newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian business elite line up behind Fiat boss.
newsitem.headline: Italian business elite line up behind Fiat boss.

text.p: The power elite of Italian business threw its weight behind Cesare Romiti, head of car giant Fiat, lashing out at his conviction for false accounting in an open letter on Thursday in Italy's top business daily.

A group of 45 businessmen, led by the honorary president of Italy's foremost merchant bank, Enrico Cuccia, and other top bankers and industrialists expressed support for Romiti in the letter, published in Milan's Il Sole 24 Ore.

"The undersigned, who know the personal commitment, the moral rectitude and orthodoxy...that have always been a characteristic of Cesare Romiti's behaviour, want on this occasion to express all their respect and their full solidarity," the letter said.
Romiti, 73, received an 18-month suspended jail sentence last week for falsifying company accounts to hide illicit payments to politicians and Fiat managers working abroad.
The sentence was passed by a court in Turin, where Fiat has its headquarters.
Turin magistrate Marcello Maddalena defended the sentence saying the court had upheld the law.
"Maybe they are amazed that we have enforced the law," Maddalena told a Milan radio station. "If they think that this is not fair they should change the law. We have to enforce it."

The letter appeared at a time when Italy's crusading magistrates, whose anti-graft investigations helped bring down a corrupt political order in the early 1990s, are coming under fire from politicians.
The opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance, led by media magnate Silvio Berlusconi, has called for accounting fraud to be decriminalised and for powers of magistrates to be reined in.

Berlusconi, who expressed sympathy with Romiti's predicament last week, himself faces several trials in Milan on charges of dressing up the accounts of his Fininvest media empire to disguise payment of bribes to politicians and civil servants.
He has said it was practically impossible to do business in Italy without falling foul of the law.

The Romiti letter hinted as much when it said the sentencing of the Fiat boss highlighted "the problem of relations between the business world and politics, relations which are all the more inevitable the bigger the companies involved".
Romiti, who is due to stand down as Fiat chairman by June next year when he turns 75, has appealed the ruling, setting in train a process that is likely to take several years to resolve.

The judge sentencing Romiti asked the public prosecutor's office to weigh up whether Fiat's honorary chairman Gianni Agnelli, who ran the group for 30 years until his retirement last year, may have a case to answer.

"Companies have good reason to be worried. This country is hyper regulated and very bureaucratic," said Sergio Romano, a former diplomat. "The temptation to cut corners is very strong in an increasingly competitive world."

Romiti was also banned from serving on a company board of directors although that sentence was also suspended. He may also have to stand trial in Rome on charges of bribing politicians for contracts to work on Rome's underground railway.
"The Romiti affair appears to have been a catalyst for the sentiments of an entire category of people," said Mario Deaglio, a commentator on economic affairs based in Turin.
Others are less than sympathetic with Romiti's plight.
Romiti's conviction has also sent shock waves through Fiat, Italy's largest industrial company, as uncertainties mount over who will take over the chairmanship when he retires.

Agnelli's nephew, Giovanni Alberto, has been groomed for a top job but his announcement at the weekend that he is being treated for a rare but curable stomach tumour appears to have cast a shadow over this plan.
